extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers, astronomers, and Royal Society readers (17th-century scientific community)
extracted.subtask_description: A scientific essay proposing and defending a physical hypothesis for the causes and timing of tides, discussing diurnal, monthly (menstrual), and annual components, and comparing the hypothesis to observations and objections. The text emphasizes empirical validation and accounting for local differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain monthly shift of tide times
rubrics_metrics.description: A hypothesis must account not only for two tides but for the observed monthly movement of the time of tides through all 24 hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galilaeo's account gives two tides always at noon and midnight, but experience shows the time of tides moves in a month's space through the whole 24 hours; any acceptable hypothesis should explain this monthly variation in timing and not fix the two tides permanently at particular hours.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility from relative masses and motions
rubrics_metrics.description: The relative sizes and gravities of bodies must make the proposed motion plausible (e.g., the earth being larger than the moon argues against the moon carrying the earth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the earth is undeniably the greater body, it is improbable that it should be carried about by the moon. Analogies with the sun and planets, and Jupiter and its satellites, are used to justify expectations about which body should move about which.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with rotational causes of satellite motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should be consistent with the idea that rotation of a primary body about its axis is the physical cause of its satellites' motion about it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sun's rotation is judged to cause primary planets' motion; similarly Jupiter's rotation explains its satellites. A tidal hypothesis should fit into this broader system of planetary motions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with the moon's synchronous aspect
rubrics_metrics.description: Any acceptable account must be compatible with the observed fact that the same side of the moon always faces the earth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The absence of observable rotation of the moon (same face toward us) is used to argue against hypotheses in which the moon carries the earth or has certain relative rotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the common centre of gravity (aggregate-body) framework
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat the earth and moon as one aggregate body moving about their common centre of gravity when estimating annual motions and their effects on tides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By statics, an aggregate of bodies is moved as its common centre of gravity is moved. The line of annual motion should be described by that common centre, and the epicyclic (menstrual) motions of the earth around that centre can explain accelerations/retardations that affect tides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for combined (diurnal + menstrual + annual) motions
rubrics_metrics.description: A sound theory must consider how diurnal (daily), menstrual (monthly), and annual motions superpose and interact to produce observed tide patterns (tide upon tide).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diurnal motion superadded to menstrual motion increases or decreases the menstrual accelerations/retardations in different surface parts, producing daily tides and explaining why the time of high water runs through 24 hours in a month; similarly, annual inequalities produce seasonal high waters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain spring and neap tides via coincidence of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: Spring tides and neap tides should be explained as arising when menstrual and diurnal accelerations/retardations coincide or cancel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When menstrual and diurnal accelerations or retardations are coincident (e.g., at new and full moons), the effect is greater (spring tides). The account emphasizes that either sudden acceleration or sudden retardation can produce a high tide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local geographical and hydrodynamic modifiers
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory must acknowledge that local features (bays, channels, gulfs, shallows, islands, currents) significantly alter tide magnitudes and timings from the open-sea ideal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author repeatedly notes that particular varieties of tides in several parts of the world cannot be derived from the general hypothesis without due consideration of these local factors; examples include bays causing delays or amplifications and vast in-draughts causing late participation in menstrual effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reconcile and test against empirical observations (diaries/records)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses should be checked against careful, location-specific observational records (diaries of high/low water with times and heights) taken over years at representative open-sea locations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author cites Romney Marsh inhabitants' consistent observations (high tides in early February and November) and contrasts them with reports from Chatham/Thames; he recommends good tide diaries from open-sea locations (Land's End, west Ireland, St. Helen's, Bermudas) to resolve discrepancies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain annual tidal variations via natural-day inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: Annual high waters should be explained by the inequality of natural days arising from solar apogee/perigee and the obliquity relation between the ecliptic and equinoctial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two causes: (1) variation in sun's daily motion near apogee/perigee (longest natural days in December, shortest in June); (2) ecliptic/equinoctial geometry causing variation near solstices/equinoxes. The combination can place the longest/shortest natural days and hence annual high waters near Candlemas and Allhallondtide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider compound interactions of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The timing and magnitude of tides may result from compound interactions (e.g., apogee/perigee with obliquity), so a sound theory must analyze how multiple causes cross or promote each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The true inequality of natural days arises from a complication of the two causes; their combination sometimes crosses and sometimes promotes each other, shifting absolute longest/shortest days and thus the annual tide times.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for observed lunar inequalities and small anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: A viable hypothesis should not conflict with, and ideally should help explain, observed small inequalities in the moon's motion that have puzzled astronomers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that considering the earth+moon common centre of gravity may explain little observed differences in planetary positions and lunar inequalities (historical difficulties Horrocks and others encountered).

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain local exceptions (e.g., East Indies quadrature tides) by local dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: When observed maxima differ (e.g., highest tides at quadratures in some East Indies locations), the general hypothesis should allow such exceptions to be explained by local geometry and long inland in-draughts delaying effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific cases like Cambaia and Pegu are explained by very large bays with vast in-draughts; tidal effects from the open sea may be felt many days after the cause, analogous to delays in straits and narrow channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use physical analogies to justify mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide physical analogies (pendulum, loose object on a moving body, water in a vessel) to illustrate how sudden accelerations or retardations of the earth's motion can cast water forward or leave it behind, producing tides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogies are used to show that both accelerative and retardative changes cause accumulations of water: a pendulum falling from a higher arch produces a larger opposite vibration; a loose thing on a moving body is left behind when the body is thrust forward and thrown forward when the body is retarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses must be empirically testable and open to correction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals are offered as conjectures to be examined, rectified if necessary, or rejected if they do not hold to observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author explicitly invites objections, recommends gathering better observations, and acknowledges the immaturity of his hypothesis, emphasizing willingness to adjust or reject it based on empirical evidence.
